warmup.q: A support agent types "Nrthwind bikes" into the merchant search. The service runs SELECT * FROM merchant WHERE lower(name) LIKE '%nrthwind%' on Oracle, with a B-tree index on name. What happens?
options: The index finds Northwind Bikes, because LIKE uses the index
Nothing is found, and Oracle reads every merchant to find out
Northwind Bikes is found, ranked first
Oracle rejects the query: LIKE needs a prefix
warmup.why: A B-tree keeps whole names in order, so it can only jump to a known prefix; a leading % means reading every row. And LIKE matches characters exactly: "nrthwind" is not in "northwind", so even the full scan finds nothing, and nothing would be ranked anyway. Words in any order, typos and ranking need an inverted index with fuzzy matching.

sections.h: Search: an inverted index maps every word to the documents that contain it
sections.html:
Support needs to find a merchant from whatever a caller says: "the Northwind bike place", or a typo like "Nrthwind". Oracle's B+tree index on name keeps whole strings in sorted order, so it can help with a prefix and nothing else. WHERE lower(name) LIKE '%bike%' reads every row, and it has no idea which match is best.

Version 1 scans: read every name and check whether it contains the words. With 2 million merchants, every keystroke reads 2 million names, and the results come back in no useful order.

Version 2 turns the data round. When a document is indexed, an analyzer splits its text into tokens (lower-cased words, here) and the store records, for every token, the list of documents that contain it, with how often. That list is a posting list, and the whole structure is an inverted index: from words to documents, the opposite of a document holding its words. A query goes through the same analyzer, then reads one posting list per query word and merges them. The cost follows the length of those lists, not the number of merchants. The first stepper builds it for five names.

A specialized store is one index shaped like one question: words to documents, time to buckets, a point to its neighbours. That's the picture for this lesson. Each store in it is fast for questions of its shape and ordinary or worse for the rest, and each one is a copy of data that lives somewhere else.

Version 3 ranks. Most search engines use BM25. For each query word in a document it adds idf x tf / (tf + k1 x (1 - b + b x length / average length)). Three ideas sit in that line. A rare word counts more than a common one: idf, the inverse document frequency. A word that appears twice counts more than once, but with diminishing returns: k1 = 1.2 caps it. A match in a short name counts more than the same match in a long description: b = 0.75 scales by length. The lab builds exactly this, and its scores match OpenSearch's to six decimal places.

Two details decide whether a search finds anything. The analyzer must be the same at index time and query time: the standard analyzer keeps bikes and bike apart, while the english one stems both to bike. And typos need fuzzy matching, which also accepts terms within one or two edits of the query word.

Which product? OpenSearch and Elasticsearch both build on the Lucene library. OpenSearch is Apache 2.0 and has been under the Linux Foundation since 2024. Elastic added AGPLv3 as a licence option for Elasticsearch in 2024, though its default download stays under the Elastic License 2.0. OpenSearch 3 also switched to Lucene's BM25, whose scores are about 2.2 times smaller than 2.x's for the same ranking, so don't compare scores across versions. For a few thousand merchants, PostgreSQL's full-text search is often enough: a GIN index is an inverted index too, as the compare block shows.

sections.h: Time-series: cut time into chunks and buckets, keep the summaries, drop the rest
sections.html:
Every card authorization records how long the card issuer took to answer. At 2,000 authorizations a second that's 173 million points a day, and the questions about them have a shape: the last hour's latency for one merchant, a 5-minute chart for the past week, a daily figure for the past year. Writes only ever append at the current time. Reads ask for a range of time, mostly recent. Old points matter only as summaries.

Version 1 is one table with a B+tree index on time. Inserts land at the right edge of the index, which is fine. Then retention: deleting a day of old rows is 173 million single-row deletes, each leaving a dead row for VACUUM ("MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM", lesson 7 of the database internals track). And the yearly chart reads about 63 billion rows to draw 365 points.

Version 2 partitions by time. TimescaleDB, a PostgreSQL extension, turns a table into a hypertable: one table to you, a chunk per time interval underneath (one per hour in the Try-it). A query for 09:00 to 10:00 opens only the chunk that holds that hour; the planner leaves the other 23 out. Retention drops whole chunks, which deletes files instead of rows. That's how add_retention_policy works.

Version 3 downsamples, the "time to buckets" part of the picture. Cut time into fixed buckets with time_bucket, and keep per bucket the count, the sum, the min and the max. Keep sums and counts rather than averages, because they add up: twelve 5-minute buckets roll up into an exact hour, while an average of averages weights a quiet five minutes the same as a busy one. A continuous aggregate keeps those summaries up to date as rows arrive. Then the raw points can expire after days while the hourly summaries stay for years.

The products: TimescaleDB keeps its name, though the company renamed itself Tiger Data in June 2025. InfluxDB 3 Core went GA in April 2025 under MIT and Apache 2.0, built in Rust on Apache Arrow and Parquet. MongoDB has time-series collections, and the Cassandra tables bucketed by day in lesson 7 of this track are the same idea done by hand.

steps: From the labs folder, start TimescaleDB: docker compose -f env/timescale.yml up -d --wait, then load one day of latencies: docker compose -f env/timescale.yml exec tsdb psql -U sfz -f /sfz/nosql-12-latency.sql (259,200 rows, a few seconds).

Open docker compose -f env/timescale.yml exec tsdb psql -U sfz and run the statements below one at a time. Predict the number of chunks, how many the 09:00 query opens, and how many hourly rows survive the retention step.

code.html: -- 1. one table to you, 24 chunks underneath: one per hour of data SELECT count(*) AS chunks FROM show_chunks('auth_latency'); -- 2. a question about 09:00 to 10:00 only opens the chunk that holds that hour EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT avg(latency_ms) FROM auth_latency WHERE time >= '2026-11-07 09:00+00' AND time < '2026-11-07 10:00+00'; -- 3. downsample: M-0042's latency in 5-minute buckets, 09:00 to 09:30 SELECT time_bucket('5 minutes', time) AS bucket, count(*) AS n, round(avg(latency_ms)::numeric, 1) AS avg_ms, round(max(latency_ms)::numeric) AS max_ms FROM auth_latency WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND time >= '2026-11-07 09:00+00' AND time < '2026-11-07 09:30+00' GROUP BY bucket ORDER BY bucket; -- 4. a continuous aggregate: hourly summaries per merchant, kept by TimescaleDB CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW latency_hourly WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', time) AS bucket, merchant_id, count(*) AS n, sum(latency_ms) AS sum_ms, max(latency_ms) AS max_ms FROM auth_latency GROUP BY bucket, merchant_id; SELECT count(*) AS hourly_rows FROM latency_hourly; -- 5. retention: drop the raw chunks from before 18:00; the hourly summaries stay SELECT count(*) AS chunks_dropped FROM drop_chunks('auth_latency', older_than => TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-07 18:00+00'); SELECT count(*) AS raw_rows FROM auth_latency; SELECT count(*) AS hourly_rows, sum(n) AS points_summarised FROM latency_hourly;

sections.h: Vectors: find the nearest neighbours by walking a graph, approximately
sections.html:
A customer writes: "charged twice for one bike rental". Support wants past disputes like it, by meaning, not by shared words. "Duplicate charge, scooter hire" should match even though it shares no word with the first. Search can't do that. An embedding can: a model turns each text into a vector, a list of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, placed so that texts with similar meanings land close together. Finding similar disputes becomes finding the nearest vectors.

Close means a small distance. Euclidean distance (L2) is the straight-line gap. Cosine distance compares only the direction. Inner product suits vectors normalized to length 1. pgvector writes them <->, <=> and <#>. Use whichever your embedding model was trained for.

Version 1 is exact: compute the distance from the query to every vector and keep the k smallest. The Try-it does that over 100,000 vectors of 32 numbers: 3.2 million multiply-adds, 2,138 pages read, about 40 ms. With 50 million disputes of 1,536 numbers each, it's 77 billion multiply-adds per query.

Version 2 would be a B+tree, and it can't work. A B+tree needs one sort order, and "close to an arbitrary point" isn't one in many dimensions: two vectors next to each other in any single order can be far apart in space.

Version 3 gives up exactness. Build a graph in which every vector links to some of its nearest neighbours, and search it by walking: start somewhere, move to whichever neighbour is closer to the query, and stop when none is. HNSW, from a 2016 paper by Malkov and Yashunin, adds layers like a skip list: a few vectors in the top layer with long links for big jumps, more in each layer below, and every vector in the bottom one. In the bottom layer the search keeps a beam of the ef best candidates rather than a single one. The second stepper walks it. In the Try-it, the HNSW index answered from 642 pages in about 3 ms.

The price is in one number: recall, the share of the true nearest neighbours that the search actually returns. With pgvector 0.8.7's defaults (m = 16 links, ef_construction = 64), the Try-it measured recall@10 of about 0.95 at hnsw.ef_search = 10 and 1.0 at 40. A bigger beam costs more distance computations. Building the index took about 26 seconds for 100,000 vectors, on a busy laptop. Filters are the other catch: a WHERE merchant_id = ? applied after the index walk can leave fewer than k rows, which is what pgvector 0.8's iterative scans address.

Vector search is turning into a feature of stores you already run: pgvector in PostgreSQL, a vector type with SAI indexes in Cassandra 5.0, vector search in MongoDB, and in DynamoDB since August 2026. If you run Postgres, start with pgvector.

try.title: Exact versus HNSW in pgvector, and the recall you pay
steps: From the labs folder, start PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector 0.8.7: docker compose -f env/pgvector.yml up -d --wait, then create 100,000 vectors of 32 numbers in 200 clusters, and 20 queries: docker compose -f env/pgvector.yml exec pgv psql -U sfz -f /sfz/nosql-12-vectors.sql (a few seconds).

Open docker compose -f env/pgvector.yml exec pgv psql -U sfz and run the block below. Predict the pages read by each plan, and the recall at ef_search 10, 40 and 200. Building the index takes about half a minute.
Stop it when you're done: docker compose -f env/pgvector.yml down -v.

code.title: in psql
code.html: -- 1. exact search: compare query 1 with every one of the 100,000 vectors EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> (SELECT embedding FROM queries WHERE id = 1) LIMIT 10; -- the true top 10 of every query, by brute force (no index exists yet) CREATE TEMP TABLE truth AS SELECT q.id AS qid, i.id FROM queries q CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.embedding LIMIT 10) i; -- 2. build an HNSW index (pgvector's defaults: m = 16, ef_construction = 64) \timing on CREATE INDEX items_hnsw ON items USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops); \timing off -- 3. the same query, through the index EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> (SELECT embedding FROM queries WHERE id = 1) LIMIT 10; -- 4. recall@10: what share of the true top 10 does the index find, at three beam widths? CREATE TEMP VIEW recall AS SELECT current_setting('hnsw.ef_search') AS ef_search, round(avg(found) / 10.0, 3) AS recall_at_10 FROM (SELECT q.id, count(t.id) AS found FROM queries q CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> q.embedding LIMIT 10) a LEFT JOIN truth t ON t.qid = q.id AND t.id = a.id GROUP BY q.id) r; SET hnsw.ef_search = 10; SELECT * FROM recall; SET hnsw.ef_search = 40; SELECT * FROM recall; SET hnsw.ef_search = 200; SELECT * FROM recall;

sections.h: Choose by the shape of the question, and count what every copy costs
sections.html:
Twelve lessons have given you one method, and it starts where lesson 2 did: write the access patterns down, then look at the shape of each question.

The question looks like Shape Store family In this track
this key, now, 20,000 times a second key lookup key-value DynamoDB (lessons 3 and 4)
this account's last 50 payments one partition, sorted sort key or wide-column DynamoDB, Cassandra (lesson 7)
a payment with its refunds, read and changed together one document document MongoDB (lesson 8)
who is linked to this account, up to 3 steps walk graph Neo4j (lesson 11)
merchants matching these words, best first words to documents search OpenSearch
p99 latency per 5 minutes for a week time range, rolled up time-series TimescaleDB
disputes like this one nearest neighbours vector pgvector
a ledger that must balance, ad-hoc reports rows, joins, invariants relational Oracle, PostgreSQL

Then check what the shape alone doesn't tell you. Does it outgrow one primary (lesson 1)? What consistency does it need, and what may it cost in latency (lesson 9)? Does an invariant span items, and what would a transaction cost (lesson 10)? Who will run it at 3 a.m., and under which licence?

Most systems end up with more than one store, and every extra store is a copy. The payments service writes the ledger in Oracle. The search index, the graph and the latency store are fed from it, usually through Kafka: an outbox table written in the same transaction, then change data capture or a consumer. That is polyglot persistence, and it has a bill. The copy lags, so a merchant created a second ago isn't searchable yet: read-your-writes, from lesson 9, is gone. A service that writes to Oracle and OpenSearch itself will one day succeed at one and fail at the other, so never dual-write: feed copies from a log. Changing an analyzer or a vector model means rebuilding the copy from that log. And each store is one more thing to patch, back up, secure and page someone about.

Start with PostgreSQL and its extensions (full-text search, TimescaleDB, pgvector) or with the store you already run, and add a dedicated store when you've measured that the question outgrows it. The families are converging, which makes that easier every year.

try.title: Place five new needs
steps: For each need, write down: the shape of the question, the store you would use, what you would key or index it by, and how its data gets there. Commit before you open the answer.

(a) Show a customer every payment they made in the last 13 months, newest first, under 50 ms. (b) Let the risk team search free-text notes on 30 million disputes, by any words. (c) Alert when a merchant's p99 authorization latency over 5 minutes passes 800 ms. (d) Suggest past disputes similar to a new one. (e) Find merchants whose payouts went to a bank account that a blocked merchant also used.
try.expect: (a) One partition, sorted: partition by account (or account and month), sort by time descending, read 50; DynamoDB with a sort key or Cassandra, fed from the payments service, or simply Oracle with an index on (account_id, created_at) if one primary keeps up. (b) Words to documents: OpenSearch, or PostgreSQL full-text search at a smaller scale; fed from the disputes database through an outbox and Kafka, with the dispute id as the document id. (c) Time range, rolled up: TimescaleDB with a continuous aggregate per 5 minutes and merchant, fed from the authorization events topic; keep max and a percentile sketch, not just the average. (d) Nearest neighbours: an embedding per dispute in pgvector next to the disputes table, HNSW index, and a recall check against exact search on a sample. (e) A walk: Neo4j with merchants and bank accounts as nodes, fed from payout events; or two joins in Oracle if it is only ever this one question. If your answer to (a) was "a new store", ask whether Oracle with the right index was already enough.

refs.title: AWS What's New: Amazon DynamoDB vector search (August 2026)

analogy: A specialized store is a reference book built for one question. A dictionary's index goes from a word to the pages it appears on: that's search. A logbook with one page per hour and a summary line at the bottom of each page, where old pages are torn out once their summary is copied into a yearly ledger, is a time-series store. A city map where every house knows its neighbours, and a quick ride on the motorway gets you to the right district before you walk the last few streets, is HNSW. The system of record is the master file, and each reference book is copied from it. The analogy breaks on freshness: a printed reference book is honestly out of date, while a database copy is a few seconds behind and looks current, so people trust it as if it were the master.
world: Look at what your payments platform already runs. Merchant search is probably a LIKE against Oracle or a search cluster someone set up years ago; the inverted index and BM25 are what make it rank. Authorization latency already lands in your metrics system, which is a time-series store with retention and downsampling; the same design applies when you keep per-merchant latency for SLA reports. Dispute handling is the obvious first use of vectors: embed the customer's text, keep it in pgvector next to the dispute rows, and show agents similar resolved cases. Feed every one of these copies from Kafka through an outbox, never by writing twice from a Quarkus service, and put the lag of each copy on a dashboard.
mistake: The most common mistake is adding a specialized store by writing to it directly from the service, next to the main write: save the merchant in Oracle, then index it in OpenSearch, in the same request handler. It works in testing, and it feels simpler than an outbox. Then one call fails or times out after the other succeeded, and the copy silently disagrees with the system of record until someone notices a merchant that can't be found. People also forget that rebuilding the copy, after a mapping or model change, needs a source to replay from. The fix: write once, to the system of record and an outbox in the same transaction, and feed every copy from that log, with the record's id as the document id and its version as an external version, so replays are idempotent and stale updates lose.

compare.title: "northwind bikes" in PostgreSQL full-text search and in OpenSearch

a.label: PostgreSQL 18: GIN index
a.title: psql
a.html: -- a GIN index is an inverted index: one entry per lexeme, pointing at the rows CREATE INDEX merchants_name_fts ON merchants USING gin (to_tsvector('english', name)); SELECT id, round(ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', name), q)::numeric, 4) AS rank FROM merchants, plainto_tsquery('english', 'northwind bikes') AS q WHERE to_tsvector('english', name) @@ q ORDER BY rank DESC; -- id | rank -- --------+-------- -- M-0042 | 0.1878

b.label: OpenSearch 3.9: match query
b.title: curl
b.html: curl -s 'localhost:9200/merchants/_search?filter_path=hits.hits._id,hits.hits._score' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "query": { "match": { "name": "northwind bikes" } } }' # {"hits":{"hits":[{"_id":"M-0042","_score":0.62533486}, # {"_id":"M-0043","_score":0.5064695},{"_id":"M-0045","_score":0.4883092}]}}

compare.note: Both are inverted indexes over the same five names, and both answers are real output (PostgreSQL 18 in a throwaway container, OpenSearch from the Try-it). plainto_tsquery requires every word, so PostgreSQL returns only M-0042; ask for either word with websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'northwind or bikes') and it returns four rows, M-0044 included, because its english stemmer turns "Bike" and "Bikes" into the same lexeme. ts_rank is not BM25: it ignores how rare a word is across the table. OpenSearch's match query is an OR of the words, ranked by BM25, with fuzzy matching and per-field analyzers to hand. For a merchant directory inside one PostgreSQL database, the first is often enough; for typo-tolerant ranked search over millions of documents, use the second.

worked.title: Feed a search index from the system of record, without dual writes

steps.say: Start from the bug. The merchant service saves to Oracle and then indexes into OpenSearch in the same handler. If the second call fails, the search never sees the merchant; if the first fails after the second succeeded, search shows a merchant that doesn't exist.
steps.code: merchantRepository.save(merchant) // 1. Oracle commits searchClient.index(merchant) // 2. a timeout here: Oracle and search now disagree

steps.say: Write once. In the same Oracle transaction as the merchant, insert an outbox row describing the change, with the merchant's version. Either both commit or neither does.
steps.code: INSERT INTO merchant (merchant_id, name, version) VALUES ('M-0042', 'Northwind Bikes', 17); INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_id, type, version, payload) VALUES ('M-0042', 'MerchantChanged', 17, '{"name": "Northwind Bikes"}'); COMMIT;

steps.say: Move the outbox to Kafka. A change-data-capture connector or a small relay reads new outbox rows and publishes them to a topic keyed by merchant id, so all changes to one merchant stay in order in one partition.

Index from the topic, idempotently. The document id is the merchant id, so a replay overwrites rather than duplicates. The Oracle version goes in as an external version, so an older event that arrives late is rejected instead of overwriting newer data.
steps.code: curl -s -X PUT 'localhost:9200/merchants/_doc/M-0042?version=17&version_type=external' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "name": "Northwind Bikes" }' # a replay of version 17, or a late version 16: a version conflict, and nothing changes

steps.say: Measure what you bought. The copy is eventually consistent: a new merchant appears after the relay, the consumer and the index refresh (every second by default). Put that lag on a dashboard, and keep the topic long enough to rebuild the index from scratch when the mapping changes.
steps.code:
lag to watch       outbox row age + consumer lag + refresh interval (1 s)
rebuild path       new index -> replay the topic -> switch an alias
never              index from the request handler

lab.title: Build an inverted index with BM25, a downsampler, and an approximate vector search
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. Three tests pass, because they test given code (tokenize, bucketStart, retain); fourteen fail.

In InvertedIndex.kt, write add (tokens, length, one posting per distinct term) and search (BM25, from the KDoc). The search test checks your scores against the ones OpenSearch returned in the Try-it. All six tests in InvertedIndexTest pass.
In TimeSeries.kt, write downsample and rollup. The rollup test gives a busy bucket and a quiet one and checks that you didn't average the averages. All six in TimeSeriesTest pass.

In VectorSearch.kt, write ExactSearch.search, then GraphIndex.search: the beam search from the stepper's last two frames. The tests build a graph over 2,000 clustered vectors and check recall@10 at different beam sizes. All seventeen pass.
Experiment: in the beam search, stop as soon as the closest candidate is farther than the BEST result instead of the worst. Watch recall fall, and put it back.
hints: add: tokens.groupingBy { it }.eachCount() gives term frequencies; postings.getOrPut(term) { mutableListOf() } += Posting(docId, tf).
search: keep a HashMap<String, Double> of scores and merge(docId, part, Double::plus). Sort with compareByDescending<Hit> { it.score }.thenBy { it.docId }.
downsample: points.groupBy { bucketStart(it.at, width) }, then build a Bucket from each group's values. rollup is the same with it.start, summing counts and sums.
Beam search: two PriorityQueues with the file's closestFirst comparator, one as is (candidates) and one closestFirst.reversed() (best, worst on top). visited.add(id) returns false if you've seen it.
Every distance(...) you compute must also do distanceCalls++: the tests check that the graph search computes far fewer than the exact one.
lab.done: All seventeen tests in InvertedIndexTest, TimeSeriesTest and VectorSearchTest pass.

drill.title: BM25 and a rollup by hand
drill.prompt: Without looking: (a) write BM25's score for one query term in one document, and say in a phrase what idf, k1 and b each do; (b) two documents contain "northwind" once each, one is 2 tokens long and the other 7, the average is 4.2: which ranks first, and why; (c) two 5-minute buckets have (count 99, sum 9,900) and (count 1, sum 900): what is the hourly average, and what would averaging the averages give?

answer.html:
(a) idf(t) * tf / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * len / avglen))
    idf = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)): rare terms count more
    k1 (1.2): saturates repeats, so the 10th occurrence adds little
    b (0.75): how much a long document is penalised for its length
(b) the 2-token one: same tf and idf, smaller length -> smaller denominator
    (0.506 against 0.313 in the lesson's five merchants)
(c) (9,900 + 900) / (99 + 1) = 108
    averaging the averages: (100 + 900) / 2 = 500, wrong, because it weights
    one quiet bucket like 99 busy ones. Keep count and sum, never the average.

recap: Search engines keep an inverted index: an analyzer turns text into terms, each term has a posting list of documents and term frequencies, and a query reads only its terms' lists. BM25 ranks by rarity (idf), saturated frequency (k1) and length (b).
Time-series stores partition by time (chunks), summarise into buckets (count, sum, min, max), roll summaries up and drop whole old chunks. Never average averages.

Vector stores find nearest neighbours of embeddings. Exact search compares with every vector; HNSW walks a layered graph with a beam of ef candidates, trading recall for speed. Measure recall@k against exact search.
Choose by the shape of the question: key, partition range, document, walk, words, time range, neighbours, or rows with invariants. Then check scale, consistency, transactions, operations and licence.

Every extra store is a copy with lag and an operational bill. Feed copies from the system of record through an outbox and a log, never by dual writes, and start with PostgreSQL and its extensions or the store you already run.

explain.prompt: A product manager asks why the payments platform needs "a search engine, a time-series database and a vector database" next to Oracle, and whether we could just use one. Explain what each one's index does that Oracle's B-tree doesn't, what each costs, and what you'd actually propose.
explain.answer: Each of those stores is one special index built for one kind of question. A search engine keeps an inverted index: for every word, the list of documents containing it, so a query reads a few lists instead of every row, and BM25 ranks the results by how rare and how concentrated the words are; Oracle's B-tree only helps with exact prefixes. A time-series store partitions by time and keeps summaries per time bucket, so a chart reads summaries instead of billions of points and old data is dropped a chunk at a time. A vector store finds the nearest embeddings, things with similar meaning, by walking an HNSW graph instead of comparing against every vector, and gives up a little recall for a large speed-up. Each one is a copy of data that Oracle owns, so each adds lag, a feeding pipeline, rebuilds when the model or mapping changes, and one more system to run. So I wouldn't buy three products. I'd start with what we have: Postgres or Oracle text search for the merchant directory, TimescaleDB or our metrics system for latency, pgvector for dispute similarity, all fed from an outbox through Kafka. I'd move one of them to a dedicated store when we measure that it outgrows that.

deeper.html:
Posting lists are compressed hard, because most of a search index is posting lists. Lucene stores document ids as gaps from the previous id, packs those small numbers into blocks of bits, and keeps skip data so that intersecting a rare term's list with a common one can jump ahead instead of reading every entry. A query for two words is then closer to a merge join with skips than to a scan. Lucene also writes its index as immutable segments, merged in the background, which should sound familiar from the LSM trees of lesson 5 of the database internals track; it's why a new document becomes searchable only after a refresh opens a new segment.

Percentiles don't roll up the way sums do. You can't combine two buckets' p99 into the hour's p99. Time-series systems keep a small sketch per bucket instead, such as a t-digest or a fixed-boundary histogram, which can be merged and then queried for any percentile with a known error. If an SLA is written as a percentile, check that your store keeps a mergeable sketch rather than a stored percentile.

HNSW isn't the only approximate index. IVF (inverted file) indexes cluster the vectors around a few hundred or thousand centroids, and a search compares the query with the centroids and scans only the nearest few clusters (ivfflat.probes in pgvector). They build faster and use less memory than HNSW, and usually need more tuning for the same recall. Product quantization shrinks each vector to a few bytes so that billions fit in memory, at more cost in recall. Whatever you pick, measure recall@k against exact search on a sample of real queries, as the Try-it did.

Graph indexes have a failure the Try-it ran into while this lesson was being written. With the vectors in 200 tight, well-separated clusters (noise of plus or minus 2 instead of 4), recall stayed at 0.90 even at ef_search = 200: two of the 20 queries found none of their true neighbours, because the search never reached their cluster from the entry point. Real embeddings are rarely that separated, but data with strong clusters, such as transactions from very different merchant categories, can split a graph into islands. More links per vector (m), or a search that starts from several entry points, are the usual remedies.

For search relevance beyond BM25, engines now combine the two worlds: hybrid search runs a BM25 query and a vector query and merges the ranked lists, for example by reciprocal rank fusion. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch both support it. It helps exactly where each fails alone: exact merchant names and ids for BM25, paraphrases for vectors.
